name: Straight Back
tagline: One taste, and you're somewhere else entirely. You always let it take you.
epigraph: The cider man also brought three liqueurs. One of them tasted like an island.
glassware: an old-fashioned glass (rocks glass), filled with crushed ice
language_row: Wren's Resonance on reading v3: ready. The line for Robin: "You can't always remember what year it was. You can remember exactly what the bread tasted like." whoYouAre cut from 245 to 181 words (the jar, the bread, the eyebrow, the warm end of the loaf and "smell this" kept). Echoes cleared: seven 4-grams in v1 (*In a Minute*'s "In London, a bartender named", *The First Guess*'s "look across the table", *Curtain Call*'s "fresh lemon and a" and others), "half a teaspoon of" (*Beside the First*), "just half a teaspoon" (*For Good*); "too much" avoided (fourteen pours have it). Pronoun warnings accepted by Wren: "he" in yours 1–4 is Dick Bradsell, never the guest. ✓
sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/bramble-dick-bradsell.md` (Robert Simonson, *A Proper Drink* pp. 5, 25, 31–32, his words; *Oxford Companion* BRAMBLE and BRADSELL pdf 335–336, from a 2011 interview, MULBERRY pdf 1368, FIX pdf 792, CLASSIC COCKTAIL pdf 473; Larousse, "mûre"; Giffard and Briottet producer pages, secondary). Drink: *A Proper Drink* p. 31 (the Bramble as printed: 60 gin, 22.5 lemon, 15 simple, 15 crème de mûre); *Flavor Matrix* BERRY pdf 52–53 (vinegar among berries' best pairings; balsamic on the chart by name). Room notes: `work/explorer-lover/`.
names_note: **Straight Back**, the room's pick (all three): his own "back in that blackberry patch", and how fast it happens ("as soon as I tried"); it claims nothing he didn't say. Tomás's caution from the bar: "straight" means neat and a "back" is a chaser, but it reads fine on a menu. Runner-up: **Here, Taste This** (Tomás; the person's gift out loud, kept off the title because it would spend whoYouAre's "smell this" and y5's handover). Also considered: *Spot-On* (reads as praise for the drink), *Somewhere Else* (repeats the tagline).
open_items: **Mûre: blackberry, not mulberry (Hester M1–M4):** *mûre* means both in French; Oxford's MULBERRY (pdf 1368) calls crème de mûre a mulberry liqueur with no source given, against Bradsell's own "blackberry patch", Oxford BRAMBLE's 2011 interview and *Proper* p. 25. The recipe says "crème de mûre (blackberry liqueur): check that the label says blackberry" (Giffard's is made from blackberry juice, "deep purple").

**Two printed specs (Hester):** *A Proper Drink* p. 31 prints ¾ oz lemon and ½ oz simple; Oxford (pdf 336) prints 30 ml lemon and rich syrup, which reads OUT on acid. The base is "the Bramble as *A Proper Drink* prints it", never "his recipe" or "his measures"; with the balsamic it's our riff.

**The shape came first (Hester):** he built the Bramble at Fred's by cutting down a Singapore Sling he'd made at the Zanzibar; the blackberry gave it its fruit, and he gave it "a more British name" (the bush, by dictionary; Oxford gives no naming motive).

**No year (Hester):** 1989 in Oxford, "1991 or '92 (Bradsell was not sure)" in *Proper*. "A modern classic": Oxford calls these "undisputed modern classics" (FIX pdf 792) and only "candidates" (CLASSIC COCKTAIL pdf 473); the reading uses the plain phrase. Fred's was a members' club, so the "strangers in his blackberry patch" are signposted.

**The balsamic (Tomás):** half a teaspoon in the drizzle (a full teaspoon reads EDGE on acid at 1.40%); plain balsamic vinegar, not a thickened glaze (glazes can carry starch). Owned neighbour: *Fair Measure*'s sherry vinegar, in a syrup. Swept at 10–35 g sugar and 8% acidity, all in range; the one edge is a crème de mûre as sweet as cassis (8.99 g vs 8.9), so the syrup follows the bottle. Crushed ice keeps melting after the strain, which Arnold's ranges don't model; the drink starts at the strong end.
**Housekeeping (Hester):** the spec's `_status` line still reads "pending Wren's ruling", and its notes cite *Matrix* pdf 52 only (pdf 53 holds the balsamic). Neither ships.
